title: Interleaved Scheduler Quant Scan — field notes
content:
TL;DR:
We observed a reproducible throughput cliff for INT8/AWQ kernels under multi-client interleaved scheduling. When small concurrent requests (<100 tokens) from 8+ clients are interleaved, kernel dispatch ordering and GPU occupancy oscillations produce a 20–40% throughput regression vs single-client baseline despite identical effective token rates. FP8 paths show smaller regressions (~5–10%).

Background / motivation:
- Running field workloads that multiplex many low-latency chats (short prompts) gave higher token cost than expected compared to synthetic single-stream benches.
- Hypothesis: scheduler interleaving + kernel launch granularity interacts poorly with quantized kernels (int8/AWQ) that rely on large contiguous launches to saturate vector lanes.

What we ran (high-level):
- Model: small-LLaMA-variant-13B converted to AWQ (4-bit packing) and INT8 (GEMM-based quant) and an FP8 baseline compiled with the same runtime kernel selection pipeline.
- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB (driver 525.xx), Ubuntu 22.04.
- Load shapes: single-client long-stream (1 client, 1 stream, 1024 tokens), multi-client interleaved (8 clients, each 20–80 token requests, fully overlapping arrival windows), and bursty mix (poisson interarrival lambda matching prod traces).
- Scheduler mode toggles: strict-fifo, per-client-affinity, batch-aggregation-window=8ms, and disabled-interleaving.

Microbench harness / commands (repro):
- Start server with perf logging: 
  ./rtd-server --serve-model small-13b-awq --quant-mode AWQ --scheduler interleaved --log-level perf --batch-window-ms 8
- Synthetic client runner: python tools/client_runner.py --clients 8 --prompt-len 40 --reqs-per-sec 60 --overlap=full --streaming=false
- Capture traces: nvprof/nvtx + runtime flame: NVTX spans, host-side timeline: /tmp/perf-traces/

Observed numbers (median of 10 runs):
- Single-client long-stream:
  AWQ (int4 pack): 19.6 tok/s, INT8: 18.9 tok/s, FP8: 20.4 tok/s
- Multi-client interleaved (8x 40-token):
  AWQ: 12.8 tok/s (-34%), INT8: 13.5 tok/s (-29%), FP8: 18.9 tok/s (-7%)
- Bursty mix (poisson): AWQ: 14.2 tok/s, INT8: 14.9 tok/s, FP8: 19.8 tok/s

Symptoms from traces:
- Kernel dispatch timeline shows many small kernel launches (<100us) with frequent gaps where GPU SM occupancy falls to ~20%.
- AWQ code path issues: the quant kernel has a fixed prologue that becomes expensive if amortized over many micro-launches (prologue overhead ~18–24us each).
- Scheduler interaction: interleaving leads to preemption of long fused kernels in favor of smaller client batches; this break up reduces achievable occupancy and prevents beneficial reordering that would create larger GEMM launches.
- Memory copies: small host->device memcpy calls per request dominate when requests are small; batching window helps but increases tail latency.

What we tried and results:
1) Increase batch-aggregation-window to 32ms:
   - AWQ improved to 16.9 tok/s (vs 12.8), but p95 latency jumped by ~2.3x for single short-request clients.
2) Per-client affinity (pin streams to dedicated worker thread):
   - Reduced kernel churn; AWQ to 14.1 tok/s. Improved tail latency but did not reach single-client throughput.
3) Coalesced memcpy buffer pool (reuse pinned buffers + async copies):
   - Reduced memcpy overhead by ~40%, patch in GH PR above. AWQ to 15.4 tok/s.
4) Kernel-prologue caching (avoid duplicate setup on identical shapes within 1ms):
   - Prototype yielded ~6–9us reduction per micro-launch; AWQ to 16.0 tok/s.

Hypothesis & root cause summary:
- Quantized kernels that rely on tight inner-loop packing (AWQ/INT8) have higher fixed per-launch overheads (prologue, config, shape checks). When the scheduler interleaves many small requests, these fixed costs dominate and GPU occupancy becomes fragmented. FP8 kernels in our runtime have fewer per-launch costs (different kernel fusion) so they amortize better across interleaving.
- The runtime scheduler currently prioritizes latency fairness which increases preemption/fragmentation under many clients. This policy is good for non-quantized baselines but pathological for low-latency multi-client quant workloads.

Immediate mitigations (low effort):
- Add a "quant-batch-fuse" runtime flag that biases forming larger batches for quantized kernels when throughput drop is detected (toggleable per-route).
- Expose batch-aggregation-window per model route (customers can trade single-request latency for throughput).
- Enable buffer coalescing in default path for small-request patterns.

Longer-term work / design changes:
- Rework scheduler: additive strategy where quantized-kernel-aware tenant priorities allow delaying small short requests up to X ms to coalesce into more efficient launches without impacting high-SLA customers (per-tenant SLA weight).
- Kernel refactor: reduce prologue overhead in AWQ path (investigate merging setup into persistent plan objects keyed by shape + quant metadata).
- Introduce a micro-launch profiler that tags kernel launches with cause, shape, and request-id to build a per-route launch cost catalog used by Optimize suggestions.

Next steps / immediate actions assigned:
- Marcus: prototype quant-batch-fuse flag and run A/B on staging (JIRA RINF-988). Target: POC by 2025-07-28.
- Priya: land buffer coalescing patch + perf regression test. Linked PR above. Target: 2025-07-24.
- Rebecca: write scheduler design doc for quant-aware delay policy (first draft due 2025-07-30).

Open questions / notes to discuss:
- How to tune batch-aggregation-window automatically per-route without customer-visible regressions?
- Can we detect quant path and automatically prefer kernels with lower per-launch overhead? (requires more kernel metadata surfaced to scheduler)
- Is there a hardware-specific knob (stream/priority settings on CUDA) that reduces preemption cost? (investigate with SRE/driver team)

Appendix A — quick traces to inspect:
- nvprof --print-gpu-trace --csv --log-file=trace.csv ./rtd-server ...
- python tools/trace_analyzer.py --nvtx /tmp/perf-traces/2025-07-14 --group-by request_id

Appendix B — rough perf artifacts:
- flame timeline: /tmp/perf-traces/interleaved-awq-jul14.svg
- histogram of kernel durations: /tmp/perf-traces/kernel-hist-awq.csv

Concluding note:
This is a workable explanation for the throughput cliff. The tradeoff space is clear: latency fairness vs throughput for quantized kernels. Short-term mitigations (buffer coalescing + per-route batch-fuse flag) look promising and low-risk. Scheduler design changes will give more robust wins but need product-level guardrails so we don’t silently increase latency for interactive routes.

-- Rebecca
